sentences: This is Caravaggio's The Calling of Saint Matthew.
In a dim room, the tax collector Matthew sits at a table with his companions, counting money.
Then someone steps in from the doorway on the right and stretches out a hand to point at him.
Caravaggio painted it between 1599 and 1600 for the Contarelli Chapel in the Roman church of San Luigi dei Francesi.
Its companion, The Martyrdom of Saint Matthew, hangs directly opposite.
The figure standing at the right is Christ, partly screened by Saint Peter in front of him.
His face is half sunk in shadow, with a thin halo just visible above his head.
Peter, too, raises a hand toward the table.
Look closely at Christ's outstretched hand, held almost loosely in the air.
It echoes Adam's hand in Michelangelo's Creation of Adam.
Linked to the idea of Christ as a second Adam, it hints that a new creation is beginning.
The light falls from an unseen source above Christ's head, not from the window.
It slices across the room on a sharp diagonal, catching the faces at the table one by one.
On the wall above, the edge between light and shadow forms a sharp slanting line.
At the middle of the table, a boy in a feathered hat turns toward the door in open surprise.
Everyone wears the clothes of Caravaggio's own day, so the Bible story seems to unfold in a Roman back street.
Beside him, a bearded man points as if to ask, "Me?"
For that reason he is usually taken to be Matthew.
His face is one of those the light touches most brightly of all.
Yet some argue that Matthew is the young man hunched over his coins at the end of the table.
Then the bearded man would be asking, "Him?"
Others think Caravaggio left it deliberately ambiguous.
At the far left, an old man in spectacles still peers down at the money.
Around one table sit those who notice the call and those who do not.
Hands that count money and a hand that calls meet in one picture.
This sharp play of bright light against deep shadow, chiaroscuro pushed to its limit, became Caravaggio's signature.
This was his first major public commission.
More than four hundred years on, the painting still hangs in the chapel it was made for.
Step back and trace the path of light once more.
Decide for yourself whom the line from Christ's hand truly reaches.
And if that hand pointed at you, how would you answer the call?
